issues.legal_issue: A court must not grant consequential interim relief on an oral application without a contemporaneous record of the application and the grounds for the order.
material_facts: A lawyer sought an interim status quo order in chambers on an oral application, undertaking to file a written application later.
There was no written application, affidavit, or contemporaneous record of the facts and submissions, and the order stated no reasons.
The order affected an auction that had already been completed and the successful bidder’s rights.
issues.conclusion: The practice of entertaining consequential oral applications and granting interim orders without any record was disapproved and forbidden under Article 141. In urgent cases, the court should at least require a skeletal written application or record the facts and submissions in its order.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 141, the Court forbade the practice of granting consequential interim relief without a record. Although formal oral applications in a matter already before the court may be permitted, urgent applications should ordinarily be supported by at least a skeletal written application; if that is impossible, the judge must make a contemporaneous record of the facts and submissions.

rule.if: consequential_interim_application and oral_application and no_written_application and no_contemporaneous_record

predicates.consequential_interim_application: A person seeks interim relief that may materially affect another person’s interests or the subject matter of a dispute.
predicates.oral_application: The request for interim relief is made orally rather than in a written application.
predicates.no_written_application: The applicant has not filed even a skeletal written application setting out the basic facts and issues.
predicates.no_contemporaneous_record: The court has made no contemporaneous record of the facts and submissions supporting the request.

issues.definition: When a person seeks consequential interim relief orally and neither a skeletal written application nor a contemporaneous court record exists, the relief must not be granted.

issues.legal_issue: Judicial hearings should be public, and a hearing in chambers is proper only when both sides are represented and the public can attend.
material_facts: The initial interim order was sought and granted in a judge’s chambers without a written application or the affected bidder being present.
The affected bidder and its representatives were waiting in court when a later hearing took place in chambers, without being informed that it would occur there.
The court was otherwise sitting in open court, and the affected bidder’s request to reconsider the continued order was declined.
issues.conclusion: The hearing procedure violated the requirement that causes generally be heard in public. A chamber sitting is permissible when both sides are represented and the sitting remains open to members of the public who wish to attend.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar v. State of Maharashtra, Scott v. Scott, and McPherson v. McPherson for the principle that public hearings support fair administration of justice and public confidence. Except for limited classes of cases, hearings must be public as a matter of law; a chamber sitting must allow both sides to be represented and the public to attend.

rule.if: judicial_cause and chambers_hearing and (not both_sides_represented or not public_accessible)

predicates.judicial_cause: A court is hearing a cause or dispute in the exercise of its judicial function.
predicates.chambers_hearing: The court hears the cause in a judge’s chambers rather than in an ordinary open courtroom.
predicates.both_sides_represented: Both sides to the cause are represented at the chamber hearing.
predicates.public_accessible: Members of the public who wish to attend can access the chamber hearing.

issues.definition: If a court hears a cause in chambers without both sides represented or without public access, the hearing must be public.

issues.legal_issue: When a court-ordered reauction fails because the highest bidder does not make the required deposit, an accepted offer from another bidder may be sanctioned as a lease subject to the required deposit.
material_facts: The court directed a fresh auction after setting aside the earlier auction.
The highest bidder at the fresh auction failed to make the required deposit within the specified time.
The appellant offered to take the shop on lease, and the administration accepted the offer.
The Court sanctioned the lease subject to the appellant making the necessary deposit.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the fresh auction and sanctioned the lease in favour of the appellant, subject to the necessary deposit.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the circumstances of the proceeding: the successful bidder at the fresh auction had failed to deposit the required amount, while the administration accepted the appellant’s offer. The judgment cites no earlier case or statutory provision for this disposition.

predicates.court_ordered_reauction: A court has directed that a fresh auction be held for the relevant property or right.
predicates.highest_bidder_failed_to_deposit: The highest bidder at the fresh auction failed to make the required deposit.
predicates.administration_accepted_alternative_offe: The responsible administration accepted another bidder’s offer to take the property or right on lease.

issues.definition: If a court-ordered reauction produces a highest bidder who fails to deposit the required amount and the administration accepts another offer, the lease may be sanctioned for that offeror subject to deposit.

issues.legal_issue: An administration may not demand an additional fee for part of a lease period when the court has confirmed a lease covering that entire period for an agreed amount.
material_facts: The Court confirmed the appellant’s lease for the entire relevant year for an agreed amount.
The administration demanded an additional prorated fee for days during that year when the appellant had operated the shop under an earlier order.
The Court found that the confirmed lease already covered those days and the entire period.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that there was no justification for the additional demand and directed that it be withdrawn.
issues.legal_principle: The Court reasoned that the confirmed lease covered the entire period at the agreed amount, leaving no basis for a further fee for days within that period. The judgment cites no earlier case or statutory provision for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_concerning_lease_demand: A court is considering an appeal that concerns an administration’s demand for a lease-related fee.
predicates.full_period_lease_confirmed: A lease covering the entire relevant period has been confirmed for an agreed amount.
predicates.extra_fee_demand_covers_period_included_: The administration demands an additional fee for days already covered by the confirmed lease.

issues.definition: If an appeal concerns a lease-related demand and the confirmed lease already covers the days for which an additional fee is demanded, the additional demand must be withdrawn.
